title: Given n pairs of parentheses, generate all combinations of well-formed (balanced) parentheses, using backtracking with constraints.

s1_definition.profdef: Given n pairs of parentheses, you must generate every string of n opening and n closing brackets that is well-formed, meaning every closer has a matching earlier opener. Backtracking builds the string character by character under two rules: you may add an opener while you still have openers left, and you may add a closer only while the number of closers placed is less than the number of openers placed. These two constraints guarantee only valid strings are ever built, so there is no wasted generation.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India generates all valid nesting patterns for approval workflows, where an opener starts a sub-approval and a closer finishes the most recent one. A clerk writes the pattern left to right. She may start a new sub-approval as long as she has not used all her allowed starts, and she may finish a sub-approval only if there is an unfinished one open. Following those two rules, every pattern she writes is automatically valid, so she never produces a nonsensical pattern that closes something never opened.
s1_definition.oneliner: Add an opener while openers remain; add a closer only while closers placed are fewer than openers placed; record when both counts reach n.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Given n pairs of parentheses, you must generate every string of n opening and n closing brackets that is well-formed, meaning every closer has a matching earlier opener. Backtracking builds the string character by character under two rules: you may add an opener while you still have openers left, and you may add a closer only while the number of closers placed is less than the number of openers placed. These two constraints guarantee only valid strings are ever built, so there is no wasted generation.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India generates all valid nesting patterns for approval workflows, where an opener starts a sub-approval and a closer finishes the most recent one. A clerk writes the pattern left to right. She may start a new sub-approval as long as she has not used all her allowed starts, and she may finish a sub-approval only if there is an unfinished one open. Following those two rules, every pattern she writes is automatically valid, so she never produces a nonsensical pattern that closes something never opened.

**One line to remember:** Add an opener while openers remain; add a closer only while closers placed are fewer than openers placed; record when both counts reach n.

sections.s2_technical:
The naive idea of generating all two-to-the-two-n strings and filtering the valid ones wastes enormous effort. The elegant approach never builds an invalid string in the first place, by enforcing the validity rules as the string grows. This is constrained backtracking, and the constraints double as pruning.

The recursion carries two counters: how many openers you have placed and how many closers. The base case is when the string length reaches two n, or equivalently both counters reach n, at which point you record the completed string. The two branching rules are the whole trick. You may place an opener whenever the opener count is less than n, because you still have openers in your budget. You may place a closer only when the closer count is strictly less than the opener count, because a closer must match an opener that was already placed and not yet closed; placing a closer when closers equal openers would close something that is not open, producing an invalid string.

Each recursive call appends one character to a StringBuilder, recurses, then removes that character to backtrack, which is the usual append-recurse-undo. Because the rules forbid invalid prefixes, every leaf of the recursion is a valid string, so the number of strings produced equals the Catalan number for n, which is far smaller than the two-to-the-two-n brute force. For n equal to three, for example, there are five valid strings, not sixty-four.

A senior-level nuance is the counting connection: the number of valid parentheses strings is the nth Catalan number, which also counts binary trees, triangulations, and many other structures, so this problem is secretly about Catalan numbers. The same constrained-generation idea, enforcing validity during construction rather than filtering afterwards, is a general technique that makes backtracking efficient and appears in generating valid expressions, balanced tag structures, and well-formed sequences.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India models nested approval workflows as balanced bracket patterns, where an opener begins a sub-approval and a closer finishes it, and the design team wants to enumerate every valid nesting shape for a given number of sub-approvals to review the possible workflow templates. This is exactly generating all valid parentheses.

Problem 2 — Every generated pattern must be well-formed, since an invalid pattern would represent a nonsensical workflow that closes a sub-approval never opened. Enforcing the two placement rules during construction guarantees validity and avoids generating and discarding garbage.

In our mini-project we build a `WorkflowShapeGenerator` that returns all valid bracket patterns for n pairs. The demo generates all shapes for three pairs and logs them.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: three pairs of parentheses, generating all valid shapes.

Step 1: Start with an empty builder, zero openers, zero closers. The opener count is below three, so we may add an opener. We append an opener, making one open, zero close.

Step 2: Still allowed another opener, append a second, two open zero close. Append a third, three open zero close. Now the opener budget is exhausted, so only closers are allowed. We append three closers in turn, producing the fully nested shape of three openers then three closers, which has length six, so we record it.

Step 3: Backtrack one closer at a time, then unwind to the point where we had two openers. There, closers are allowed because closers placed are fewer than openers placed, so we append a closer, giving two open one close, then explore adding an opener again, weaving the brackets.

Step 4: This weaving produces shapes like opener opener closer opener closer closer, and opener opener closer closer opener closer, each recorded when length reaches six.

Step 5: Backtracking further to one opener yields shapes that start by closing early, such as opener closer opener opener closer closer and opener closer opener closer opener closer.

Step 6: After exploring every legal branch, exactly five valid shapes are produced, the Catalan number for three, and every one is well-formed because the two placement rules never allowed an invalid prefix.

```
[2026-10-26 23:37:01] INFO    Valid shapes for 3 pairs: 5
[2026-10-26 23:37:01] INFO      shape: ((()))
[2026-10-26 23:37:01] INFO      shape: (()())
[2026-10-26 23:37:01] INFO      shape: (())()
[2026-10-26 23:37:01] INFO      shape: ()(())
[2026-10-26 23:37:01] INFO      shape: ()()()
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Generate Parentheses (Constrained Backtracking) ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Constrained generation (only valid prefixes built)           │
  │  Counters (open, close) prune invalid branches                │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ───────────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: WorkflowShapeGenerator only enumerates valid shapes       │
  │  O: generalises to k bracket types with same rule pattern     │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ────────────────────────────────────────

  ┌───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │         WorkflowShapeGenerator        │
  │  ──────────────────────────────────── │
  │  + generate(n): List<String>          │  Catalan(n) outputs
  │  - backtrack(sb, open, close, n, res) │  rule-guarded append
  └───────────────────────────────────────┘
      Invariant: every prefix is a valid partial string

  ── State Diagram: Build ─────────────────────────────────

  [open < n] ──→ append '(' , recurse, undo
  [close < open] ──→ append ')', recurse, undo
  [len == 2n] ──→ record (leaf)

  ── Call Chain ────────────────────────────────────────────

  1. generate(n) → backtrack("", 0, 0, n)
  2.   len==2n → record
  3.   if open<n: append '(' recurse undo
  4.   if close<open: append ')' recurse undo
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Given n pairs of parentheses, I must generate every well-formed string of n openers and n closers, where every closer matches an earlier opener. The naive approach of generating all two-to-the-two-n strings and filtering the valid ones wastes huge effort, so instead I build only valid strings in the first place using constrained backtracking, where the validity rules themselves act as the pruning.

The recursion carries two counters, how many openers I have placed and how many closers, and the base case records the string once its length reaches two n. The two branching rules are the entire trick. I may place an opener whenever I still have openers in my budget, meaning the opener count is below n. I may place a closer only when the closer count is strictly less than the opener count, because a closer must match an opener that is already placed and not yet closed; closing when the counts are equal would close something that is not open. Each call appends one character, recurses, and removes it to backtrack. Because invalid prefixes are never allowed, every leaf is a valid string, and the number produced is the nth Catalan number, which for three pairs is just five, far fewer than the sixty-four brute-force strings.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this to enumerate valid nesting shapes for nested approval workflows, where an opener begins a sub-approval and a closer finishes it, so the design team could review every possible workflow template for a given number of sub-approvals. Enforcing the two rules during construction guaranteed every template was well-formed and avoided generating and discarding nonsensical shapes.

The senior-level point I make is that this problem is secretly about Catalan numbers, since the count of valid strings is exactly the nth Catalan number, which also counts binary trees and polygon triangulations, so recognising it signals mathematical maturity. More practically, I highlight the general technique on display: enforcing validity during construction rather than filtering afterwards is what makes backtracking efficient, and it is the same idea I apply when generating valid expressions, balanced tag structures, and other well-formed sequences.
